title: The Behaviour and Captivation of the Animal; the Disinhibiting Ring; the Concluding Delimitation of the Organism (Driesch & Uexküll); Being-Open in Captivation as a Not-Having of World

work.full: The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics: World, Finitude, Solitude

location.page_offset_formula: pdf = floor((book_page + 24) / 2); read GA from running heads (non-linear)

spine_role: The conceptual core of the 'animal poor in world' arc: it gives captivation (Benommenheit) its full structure, introduces the disinhibiting ring (Enthemmungsring), credits the two decisive biological steps (Driesch's wholeness, Uexküll's Umwelt), and resolves the having/not-having-world aporia by showing captivation grounds poverty in world (not the reverse). For the boredom index it supplies the privative counter-image against which Dasein's world-formation — and the boredom that discloses world 'as a whole' — is defined.

key_terms.gloss: Benommenheit — the essential structure of animality: the animal is 'taken/dazed', held within itself such that any apprehending of something as something is withheld from it. Not a transient state but the inner possibility of all behaviour.
Benehmen / Sichbenehmen — the specific manner of being of the animal (drive, a driven performing), opposed to human comportment (Verhalten) as action.
Verhalten — the specific manner of being of man as action/self-directed comporting-toward, set against the animal's mere behaviour.
Treiben — behaviour is not a doing and acting but an instinctual drivenness, a driven performance.
Eingenommenheit in sich — the animal's intrinsic self-retention and being-absorbed-in-itself that is the basis of behaviour (no reflection involved).
Hingenommenheit / hingenommen — the animal is 'taken' by its food / by things; captivated being-taken excludes taking up a position over against what takes it.
Vernehmen — apprehending something as something; precisely what is withheld (genommen) from the animal. The animal can behave (sich benehmen) but never apprehend (vernehmen).
Enthemmungsring — the encircling sphere the animal draws about itself which prescribes what can affect/occasion its behaviour; the animal bears it along as long as it lives.
Enthemmung — that which initiates/releases the inhibited instinctual drive into driven activity; that which disinhibits constantly withdraws (entzieht sich) and is never attended to as such.
Sich-Einringen / self-encircling open to disinhibition — not an encapsulation but the opening of a sphere within which whatever disinhibits can do so; the fundamental capability of the animal.
Umringen / umringt / Umringung — the animal is encircled by the ring of the reciprocal drivenness of its drives, which it cannot escape and within which something is open for it.
Ringen — life is nothing but the animal's encircling itself and struggling with its encircling ring; an essential character of life (self-preservation, maintenance of species).

Beseitigen — behaviour is intrinsically a form of elimination / leaving-to-one-side; shows itself as devouring or as avoidance; must be taken in a fundamental sense, since no letting-be of beings occurs at all.
Weltarmut / arm an Welt — the guiding thesis ('the animal is poor in world'); on the basis of being-open it can be deprived; yet poverty is 'roughly put, nonetheless a kind of wealth'.
Weltbildung / weltbildend — man's world-forming, against which the animal's poverty in world is set in the comparison.

Umwelt — Uexküll's 'environing world'; Heidegger says it 'means nothing other than' what he has characterized as the disinhibiting ring, but the comparison becomes problematic if the human world is spoken of the same way.
Innenwelt — the second term of Uexküll's title (Umwelt und Innenwelt der Tiere); not to deter us from pursuing what he means.
abbauend — the essence of life becomes accessible only if considered in a deconstructive [abbauenden] gaze; life is not thereby inferior to human Dasein but a domain with a wealth of openness.
Eigentum / bei sich selbst — the formal selfhood of the animal as being-proper in all its driven activity; yet it is absorbed without ever being 'with itself' (bei sich selbst) in the proper sense.

Reizbarkeit — the distinctive characteristic of 'living substance' (Johannes Müller); Heidegger inverts the standard order: stimulation is possible only where there is already disinhibition and intrinsic encirclement.
Driesch's biological theory appealing to a force or entelechy; repudiated by biology today; vitalism is 'just as dangerous as mechanism' — it tries to solve the problem of purposiveness too hastily.
Ganzheit — the holistic character of the organism (Driesch's 'first step'): the organism is not an aggregate of parts but governed by wholeness at every stage; already recognized by Aristotle.

oikos — the Greek word for 'house', from which 'ecology' derives; ecology = the investigation of where and how animals are at home in the world (Uexküll's domain), but mis-taken in Darwinism as adaptation.

claims.text: The animal's manner of being is behaviour (Benehmen), a driven performing; man's manner of being is comportment (Verhalten), an action. They are 'fundamentally different from one another'.

Captivation is the condition of possibility for the fact that the animal behaves within an environment but never within a world; it is not a transient or permanent state but the inner possibility of animal being itself.

The bee that carries on sucking while its abdomen is cut away proves it does not recognize the presence of too much honey; it is simply 'taken [hingenommen] by its food', and such driven being-taken excludes any recognition of presence.

The captivation of the animal signifies, first, having every apprehending of something as something withheld (genommen) from it, and, second, in this withholding, being precisely taken (hingenommen) by things.
Beings are neither disclosed to nor closed off from the animal: captivation stands outside that possibility; 'the animal as such does not stand within a manifestness of beings.'
Behaviour has an eliminative character (Beseitigen): the animal is never there for the other simply as a living creature but only as sexual partner or as prey — in some form of 'away' (weg).
The animal surrounds itself with a disinhibiting ring (Enthemmungsring) that prescribes what can affect or occasion its behaviour; nothing else can ever penetrate the ring around the animal.

Stimulation is not the condition of disinhibition; on the contrary, 'it is only where there is disinhibition and intrinsic encirclement that stimulation is possible' — reversing the standard physiological order.

Positively expressed, the organism is the capability for behaviour in the unity of captivation; the unity of the animal's body is grounded in the unity of captivation, i.e. in self-encirclement with a disinhibiting ring. 'Captivation is the fundamental essence of the organism.'

Captivation has six structural moments: [1] withholding; [2] being taken; [3] absorption; [4] openness for something else; [5] the structure of encirclement thus given; [6] captivation as the condition of the possibility of any behaviour.
Driesch's sea-urchin embryology established the breakthrough of wholeness (the first decisive step), but drove him to neovitalism (entelechy); vitalism is 'just as dangerous as mechanism'.

Uexküll's investigations are the second decisive step; his 'environing world' (Umwelt) 'means nothing other than' what Heidegger calls the disinhibiting ring — yet the engagement with such concrete investigations is 'one of the most fruitful things that philosophy can learn from contemporary biology'.

The decisive problem is not the qualitative/quantitative otherness of the animal world but whether the animal can apprehend something as something, something as a being, at all; if it cannot, it is separated from man 'by an abyss'.

Captivation is at the same time motility (Bewegtheit): not a static framework but an intrinsically determinate motility that continually unfolds or atrophies; this belongs to the essence of the organism, and the interpretation is incomplete until the life-process (and death) is taken into account.

The animal has access to beings (the nest, the prey) but cannot have world: world is the accessibility of beings as such, and in captivation the possibility of the manifestness of beings as such is withheld.

We find not a simultaneous having and not-having of world but a not-having of world in the having of openness for whatever disinhibits — a 'not-having' on the basis of a 'having' that the stone wholly lacks.

Heidegger's self-objection: if the world is essentially closed to the animal we may speak of a not-having but never of a deprivation, since deprivation presupposes at least some knowledge of world; so the poverty-thesis 'goes too far' and is conceived only by comparison with man.

Removal of the objection: captivation (not poverty in world) is the condition of the possibility of poverty in world; the poverty-thesis is at best a 'merely comparative' definition from the human perspective, far from being a, let alone the, fundamental metaphysical principle of animality.

The thesis must be retained as a problem: that which disinhibits brings 'an essential disruption into the essence of the animal', and the question of the animal's not-having of world was developed under the guidance of the fundamental attunement of profound boredom, which manifests the 'as a whole' to us.

interlocutors.name: Hans Driesch
interlocutors.note: First decisive step in biology: sea-urchin embryology (Die Lokalisation morphogenetischer Vorgänge, 1899) establishes wholeness; but Driesch's neovitalism (entelechy) is repudiated. Vitalism 'just as dangerous as mechanism'.

interlocutors.name: Jakob Johann von Uexküll
interlocutors.note: Second decisive step: research on how the animal is bound to its environment (Umwelt und Innenwelt der Tiere, 2nd ed. 1921; Theoretische Biologie). Umwelt = Heidegger's disinhibiting ring; cited in the bee-footnote (Theoretische Biologie p.141) and the phototropism footnote (Umwelt p.207).

interlocutors.name: Johannes Müller
interlocutors.note: Physiologist (Handbuch der Physiologie des Menschen, 1844); identified irritability (Reizbarkeit) as the mark of 'living substance'; Heidegger uses him to argue stimulation is grounded in prior disinhibition.

interlocutors.name: Emanuel Rádl
interlocutors.note: Untersuchungen über den Phototropismus der Tiere (1905); explained the bee-experiments of Bethe; cited for freshwater-crab phototropism (via Uexküll). Light-seeking ≠ grasping the light as such.

interlocutors.name: F. J. J. Buytendijk
interlocutors.note: Dutch biologist; Heidegger contests his claim that the animal's bond to environment is 'almost as intimate as the unity of the body itself' — for Heidegger the body's unity is grounded in the unity of captivation.

interlocutors.name: Karl Ernst von Baer
interlocutors.note: Embryologist 'of the grand style' who saw something essential in the first half of the 19th century, buried by Darwinism; the same figure BT §12 names as the biological source of 'Umwelt'.

interlocutors.name: Hans Spemann
interlocutors.note: His 'equally outstanding' investigations set Driesch's developmental result on a new basis, turning the problem of animal development in a new direction.

interlocutors.name: Theodor Boveri
interlocutors.note: Die Organismen als historische Wesen (1906); cited as having attempted to talk about organisms as historical beings — raised to ask what 'history' the species/individual animal possesses.

interlocutors.name: Charles Darwin / Darwinism
interlocutors.note: Darwin's moth-and-candle question is invoked re phototropism; Darwinism's externalized concept of 'adaptation' and self-preservation (an 'economic perspective upon man') is repeatedly criticized as misleading.

interlocutors.name: St. Paul / Apocrypha (4 Ezra)
interlocutors.note: Romans VIII.19 (apokaradokia tes ktiseos — the 'yearning expectation of creatures'); 4 Ezra IV.7,12; cited at the close to gesture toward suffering/yearning in creation, while insisting biology knows nothing of it and metaphysics is not thereby silenced.

bridge_relevance: fcm-12 is the privative anchor of the boredom spine. Profound boredom (Part One) is what discloses the 'as a whole' and lets man's world-formation be questioned; this unit supplies the contrast term — the animal that is captivated, ringed by disinhibition, and therefore poor in world. Two structural transfers matter for the King–Salvo pipeline. (1) The disinhibiting-ring / openness-without-manifestness structure models 'engagement without world-disclosure': the captivated animal is intensely related-to and absorbed-by its environment yet apprehends nothing as such — a precise philosophical analogue of the eye-tracking digest's 'engaged surface' (gaze locked, occupied) over a 'bored depth' (no disclosure of the situation as such). (2) Heidegger's inversion (stimulation presupposes prior disinhibition, not vice versa) parallels the bridge's grid-not-scale recommendation: receptivity is a function of the encompassing attunement/ring, not of stimulus intensity — so a deliberately boring stimulus does not produce boredom additively but discloses (or fails to disclose) a situation 'as a whole'. The Uexküll engagement also licenses the dissertation's own Wirkton/affordance synthesis (see the companion BT/FCM report). All such mappings are anticipatory-application; the transcription itself is faithful to FCM.
